title: urnetwork / lag.dev
description: lag.dev measurements: how many are made and how they end, the traffic and refusals at the lag routes, the latency and speeds measured, the extenders taking part, where visitors come from, and the retention sweep (lag.dev/PLAN.md X9). Measurements from agent browsers and hosting networks are left out of every panel but their own (amendment 12). No series names a visitor, an address or an extender.

panels.title: measurements per hour
panels.description: lag.dev results stored in the trailing hour, stacked by how the measurement ended: complete is a full minute with its download and upload; client_closed is a load the browser gave up (a hidden page); no_load and busy are a minute without a load. Counted from the database every 5 minutes, so the figure survives restarts. The stats collector runs in every taskworker and each publishes the same database count, so this reads the gauge with max across hosts rather than a bare series; series are per process and keyed by instance, and during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: measurements, last hour
panels.description: Every lag.dev result stored in the trailing hour, whatever its end reason. A healthy visit stores 8, one per dot. The stats collector runs in every taskworker and each publishes the same database count, so this reads the gauge with max across hosts rather than a bare series; series are per process and keyed by instance, and during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: measurements per hour by address family
panels.description: The same trailing-hour results split by the family the browser reached its extender on (ipv4 or ipv6). Only the family is ever stored, never an address (amendment 9). The stats collector runs in every taskworker and each publishes the same database count, so this reads the gauge with max across hosts rather than a bare series; series are per process and keyed by instance, and during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: measurements per hour by source
panels.description: The headline's measurements by the client that ran them: web is lag.dev in a browser, cli and mcp the lagdev command line and MCP server, which name themselves with an X-Lag-Client header. All three count in every panel; automated tracks are left out here as there. A database count every taskworker publishes, read with max across hosts.

panels.title: tracks and guest sessions per hour
panels.description: Tracks started and guest sessions created in the trailing hour, from the database. A visit is one guest session for a day and one track per run, so tracks above sessions means visitors pressing +. The stats collector runs in every taskworker and each publishes the same database count, so this reads the gauge with max across hosts rather than a bare series; series are per process and keyed by instance, and during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: report outcomes per hour
panels.description: Each report an extender posted, accepted or rejected by reason: malformed, extender (not the poster's own), signature, ticket (unknown, mismatched, or its track already swept), bounds, duplicate. A steady rejected_signature or rejected_ticket from many extenders points at a release mismatch. Counted by the api's lag handlers and read as increase() over the trailing hour, summed across processes: every series is per process and keyed by instance, so the sum adds each process's own increase and a redeploy neither double counts nor reads as a reset.

panels.title: abuse-limit refusals per hour
panels.description: Requests the abuse limits refused: guest sessions and tracks over their per-network or per-client limits (A1, A6), and report posts over an extender's rate (a 429 its reporter retries with backoff). A per-/24 limit is shared by everyone on that network, so a burst here is not always one visitor. Counted by the api's lag handlers and read as increase() over the trailing hour, summed across processes: every series is per process and keyed by instance, so the sum adds each process's own increase and a redeploy neither double counts nor reads as a reset.

panels.title: request outcomes per hour
panels.description: Every answer the lag routes gave, by outcome: sessions and tracks created, reissued, refused by a limit, unavailable (nothing to measure, or tickets cannot be signed), rejected (a 4xx) or error; report posts processed, rate limited, rejected or error. unavailable tracks with no refusals usually means no extender is offered. Counted by the api's lag handlers and read as increase() over the trailing hour, summed across processes: every series is per process and keyed by instance, so the sum adds each process's own increase and a redeploy neither double counts nor reads as a reset.

panels.title: automated measurements per hour, left out
panels.description: Measurements in the trailing hour from automated tracks, which every other panel leaves out (amendment 12): signature_agent is an agent browser that signs its requests (Web Bot Auth's Signature-Agent), and datacenter_asn an address in a hosting or cloud network, Cloudflare's WARP included. Normal is a small share of the headline; a rise means agents or crawler renderers are running the test. Only the flag is stored, never an address or an agent's name. A database count every taskworker publishes, read with max across hosts.

panels.title: idle latency p50
panels.description: Idle latency as lag.dev shows it (L4): a dot's pings whose round trip overlaps no load of any dot in its track, from the load's first byte to 2 s after its upload, derived from each result's minute and its track's load windows when the stats refresh. Loads run back to back, so a dot's minute holds its neighbours' loads as well as its own, and those pings are not idle. Over the trailing hour's complete results only (a load given up has no speeds), the median of each result's own idle p50, split by family. A family with no complete result in the hour has no line rather than a zero. The stats collector runs in every taskworker and each publishes the same database count, so this reads the gauge with max across hosts rather than a bare series; series are per process and keyed by instance, and during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: download p50
panels.description: Download speed: Over the trailing hour's complete results only (a load given up has no speeds), the median of each result's own p50, split by family. A family with no complete result in the hour has no line rather than a zero. The stats collector runs in every taskworker and each publishes the same database count, so this reads the gauge with max across hosts rather than a bare series; series are per process and keyed by instance, and during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: upload p50
panels.description: Upload speed: Over the trailing hour's complete results only (a load given up has no speeds), the median of each result's own p50, split by family. A family with no complete result in the hour has no line rather than a zero. The stats collector runs in every taskworker and each publishes the same database count, so this reads the gauge with max across hosts rather than a bare series; series are per process and keyed by instance, and during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: extenders offered
panels.description: Extenders the lag.dev sample can offer now: an issued certificate whose name is published (C8) and which A8 has handed to the extender, active addresses, a place to pick them by, and no restart loop: four activation passes of both families within two hours, the last less than two hours ago (A4). A new extender is counted from its first certificate poll after issuance, up to half an hour after its name is published. Zero means every new track answers unavailable. The stats collector runs in every taskworker and each publishes the same database count, so this reads the gauge with max across hosts rather than a bare series; series are per process and keyed by instance, and during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: measurement requests by state
panels.description: Extenders' measurement certificate requests (A10): pending waits on the weekly certificate cap, issued serves, refused failed a check, withdrawn was taken out (deactivated, gated, a canary, or opted out). The stats collector runs in every taskworker and each publishes the same database count, so this reads the gauge with max across hosts rather than a bare series; series are per process and keyed by instance, and during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: opted out
panels.description: Extenders whose owner turned measurement off (SetMeasurementsEnabled, connectctl --no_measurement, or the app's lag.dev speed tests switch); their names were withdrawn (C4, C9). The stats collector runs in every taskworker and each publishes the same database count, so this reads the gauge with max across hosts rather than a bare series; series are per process and keyed by instance, and during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: extender participation

targets.legendFormat: in a restart loop, not offered

panels.description: Extenders offered beside the requests by state over time, so a drop in offered extenders can be read against issuance and withdrawals, and beside the extenders that serve but are left out because they are in a restart loop now, or because the measurement api probes failed on every family they probed, twice in a row or more (A4). An extender both counts as restarting, so offered, restarting and unreachable add up to the extenders that serve. The stats collector runs in every taskworker and each publishes the same database count, so this reads the gauge with max across hosts rather than a bare series; series are per process and keyed by instance, and during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: visitors by country, last day
panels.description: lag.dev visitors (one guest session per browser for a day) who started a track in the trailing day, by the country of the track's place: the top 10 and other, so the label stays bounded. The place is looked up from the request in memory and no address is kept (amendment 9). The stats collector runs in every taskworker and each publishes the same database count, so this reads the gauge with max across hosts rather than a bare series; series are per process and keyed by instance, and during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: rows the sweep removed per hour
panels.description: What the lag sweep removed (A2, A5): expired guest networks after their day, tickets after 48 h, and results and their tracks after the 7 day retention. A flat zero for a day while measurements arrive means the sweep has stopped. Counted by the taskworker and read as increase() over the trailing hour, summed across processes, which are keyed by instance.

panels.title: probes by outcome
panels.description: The latest measurement api probe of each extender's family by outcome, among those recent enough for the sample to read (A4): ok, what failed, or unprobed. A lot of unprobed means the prober held a family's failures to be its own fault, or has no route to it, and those extenders are offered unjudged. All of them at 0 means the chain has stopped. The stats collector runs in every taskworker and each publishes the same database reading, so this reads the gauge with max across hosts rather than a bare series; series are per process and keyed by instance, and during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: age of the newest probe
panels.description: How long ago any extender was last probed. It stays under about 2 minutes while the chain runs. From 15 minutes the sample reads no probe and offers every extender, with the unreachable gauge at 0, so this is what shows the chain has stopped. The stats collector runs in every taskworker and each publishes the same database reading, so this reads the gauge with max across hosts rather than a bare series; series are per process and keyed by instance, and during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: probe guard trips per hour
panels.description: Passes in which most of a family failed, at least three addresses, so the prober held it to be its own fault and recorded the failures unprobed rather than failed (lagprobe.ProbeAll). The unreachable gauge reads 0 meanwhile. One now and then is a moment of the taskworker's own network; a run of them means the probes are blind to that family. A recheck has no such guard. The counter is per process, so this is summed across processes through increase().

panels.title: drift runs and verdicts per day
panels.description: Drift test runs started, and verdicts computed, in the trailing day (lag.dev/DRIFTTEST.md P7). During market discovery nothing is billed, and the tables keep 7 days, so these counters are the record of usage (ops/drift-test.md 7). A verdict is recomputed after every completed run from the token's last 3 counting runs (V7), so a test adds one per completed run: agree is Pass, disagree is Reject, inconclusive is neither. The api counts a run at its start; whichever process completes it counts the verdict: the api as reports arrive and as tests are read, or the taskworker's sweep. Counted per process, whose series are keyed by instance, and read as each process's count over the window, summed: its last value in the window less its last value before it, or its whole value when it began within the window. A drift counter's series starts at its first count in a process, which an increase cannot see, and a process that started and stopped within the window would be lost by reading only the current series; drift counts are small, so this counts every one.

panels.title: drift tests by network, last day
panels.description: Runs started and verdicts computed in the trailing day, for the 10 networks with the most runs (topk), so the table stays bounded however many networks enable Embed. A network here is an Embed customer's (P7), never a visitor's. A blank verdict cell is none. Mostly inconclusive for one network is its integration, such as the wrong client_ip, or its audience; ops/drift-test.md 7.1 and 7.2 break it down from the tables, and name the network. Counted per process, whose series are keyed by instance, and read as each process's count over the window, summed: its last value in the window less its last value before it, or its whole value when it began within the window. A drift counter's series starts at its first count in a process, which an increase cannot see, and a process that started and stopped within the window would be lost by reading only the current series; drift counts are small, so this counts every one.

targets.expr: sum by (network_id) ((last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_verdicts_total{env="$env",verdict="agree"}[1d]) - last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_verdicts_total{env="$env",verdict="agree"}[1d] offset 1d)) or last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_verdicts_total{env="$env",verdict="agree"}[1d])) and on (network_id) topk(10, sum by (network_id) ((last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_runs_total{env="$env"}[1d]) - last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_runs_total{env="$env"}[1d] offset 1d)) or last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_runs_total{env="$env"}[1d])))

sum by (network_id) ((last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_verdicts_total{env="$env",verdict="disagree"}[1d]) - last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_verdicts_total{env="$env",verdict="disagree"}[1d] offset 1d)) or last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_verdicts_total{env="$env",verdict="disagree"}[1d])) and on (network_id) topk(10, sum by (network_id) ((last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_runs_total{env="$env"}[1d]) - last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_runs_total{env="$env"}[1d] offset 1d)) or last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_runs_total{env="$env"}[1d])))

sum by (network_id) ((last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_verdicts_total{env="$env",verdict="inconclusive"}[1d]) - last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_verdicts_total{env="$env",verdict="inconclusive"}[1d] offset 1d)) or last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_verdicts_total{env="$env",verdict="inconclusive"}[1d])) and on (network_id) topk(10, sum by (network_id) ((last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_runs_total{env="$env"}[1d]) - last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_runs_total{env="$env"}[1d] offset 1d)) or last_over_time(urnetwork_lag_drift_runs_total{env="$env"}[1d])))

panels.title: drift verdict mix per hour
panels.description: Verdicts computed in the trailing hour, stacked by verdict and reason (P4, V6), counted with each verdict. agree inside_ip_country is the bulk; agree region_overlaps rises as ellipses widen; disagree region_outside follows the customers' audiences, such as VPNs. inconclusive by why: low_precision, no extenders near; too_few_extenders, sessions failing; inconsistent, the speed-of-light check, so misplaced extenders or a broken path (ops/drift-test.md 9.2, and LagDriftInconsistentSpike); ip_mismatch, the wrong client_ip; ip_family_mismatch; ip_country_unknown, a code the border file lacks, or a process without the file; reports_missing and stopped_early (the outcome panels below). A step that starts with a calibration, a border file or a release points at it (ops 6, 5, 7.2). Counted per process, whose series are keyed by instance, and read as each process's count over the window, summed: its last value in the window less its last value before it, or its whole value when it began within the window. A drift counter's series starts at its first count in a process, which an increase cannot see, and a process that started and stopped within the window would be lost by reading only the current series; drift counts are small, so this counts every one.

panels.title: drift run stops per hour
panels.description: Runs completed in the trailing hour, stacked by the browser's stop (V10): converged, the usual, about 3 to 5 s in; clear, a decisive result; interrupted, no pong from any extender for 4 s; cap, 12 s without a steady estimate; none, a frame that never called finish (the tab closed), so the run moved to processing 30 s after its start, and a small share is normal. More cap after a lag.dev or SDK release is a regression in the frame's stop rule; more interrupted is extenders going quiet mid-run, or visitors' networks dropping the sessions (ops/drift-test.md 7.3). Counted per process, whose series are keyed by instance, and read as each process's count over the window, summed: its last value in the window less its last value before it, or its whole value when it began within the window. A drift counter's series starts at its first count in a process, which an increase cannot see, and a process that started and stopped within the window would be lost by reading only the current series; drift counts are small, so this counts every one.

panels.title: drift run outcomes per hour
panels.description: Runs completed in the trailing hour, stacked by outcome (E5, K3, K4, V10), decided in this order: ip_mismatch, started from another /29 (/56) than client_ip; reports_missing, fewer than 6 sessions reported by report_wait_ms; ip_family_mismatch, most sessions took the start's other family; too_few_extenders, fewer than 6 usable reports; stopped_early, the reports support no stop where the browser stopped; else counted. Only counted runs enter a verdict, but every run uses one of the token's 6. Mostly ip_mismatch for every network is the api seeing the wrong address for start; for one, its client_ip (ops/drift-test.md 7.1, 3.3). Counted per process, whose series are keyed by instance, and read as each process's count over the window, summed: its last value in the window less its last value before it, or its whole value when it began within the window. A drift counter's series starts at its first count in a process, which an increase cannot see, and a process that started and stopped within the window would be lost by reading only the current series; drift counts are small, so this counts every one.

panels.title: drift runs reports_missing or stopped_early per hour
panels.description: The two run outcomes that point at the platform rather than a customer (ops/drift-test.md 7.3). reports_missing: fewer than 6 sessions reported by report_wait_ms; everywhere at once, report posts failing or rejected (the report outcome panels above) or real tickets carrying NoReport after a deploy; in one network, its audience blocks extenders or someone scripts its tokens. stopped_early: the signed reports support no stop where the browser stopped (V10); a small rate is clock skew between browsers and extenders; in one network, a custom client stopping at a lucky moment; everywhere after a release, a parity break between the frame's rules and the server's (V9). Counted per process, whose series are keyed by instance, and read as each process's count over the window, summed: its last value in the window less its last value before it, or its whole value when it began within the window. A drift counter's series starts at its first count in a process, which an increase cannot see, and a process that started and stopped within the window would be lost by reading only the current series; drift counts are small, so this counts every one.

panels.title: drift processing latency, finish to complete
panels.description: How long a verdict took after the frame finished its run (E5): p50, p90 and p99 over the trailing hour, of runs the frame finished; a run without a finish is left out, as in ops/drift-test.md 7.4. Under 2 s when every opened session's extender reports promptly (ReportPromptly, E4); a hump near 10 s is extenders without it, whose batch timer sends the report, and it shrinks as they update (ops 8); a wall at 20 s is runs completed by report_wait_ms with reports missing; over 35 s, report_wait_ms plus a sweep, is stuck (ops 9.1). The lines mark 20 s and 35 s. Each process's histogram buckets are counted as the counters are, and summed by bucket.

panels.title: drift runs stuck and tests failed

targets.expr: max(urnetwork_lag_drift_stuck_runs{env="$env",service="taskworker"} and on (env, service, block, host, instance) topk(1, urnetwork_lag_drift_sweep_timestamp_seconds{env="$env",service="taskworker"}))

panels.description: Runs stuck: runs still started or processing a minute past their report wait (E5), as the drift sweep's newest pass found them. Each taskworker keeps the count of the last pass it ran, so this reads the count of the taskworker whose pass ended last. Any is ops/drift-test.md 9.1: a process without the border file, lock waits on lag_drift_test rows, or Main's health; LagDriftRunsStuck warns after 5 minutes. Tests failed: drift tests marked failed by an internal error in the trailing hour (P4), each logged as [lag]drift test <id> failed; a failed test closes its open runs as failed, so they never count as stuck. One is a bug to chase and a burst is ops 9.1, and LagDriftTestFailed warns on any. Counted per process, whose series are keyed by instance, and read as each process's count over the window, summed: its last value in the window less its last value before it, or its whole value when it began within the window. A drift counter's series starts at its first count in a process, which an increase cannot see, and a process that started and stopped within the window would be lost by reading only the current series; drift counts are small, so this counts every one.

panels.title: drift demo starts per hour
panels.description: Starts of the demo token, lag.dev/?t=demo (W8), beside real tokens' starts for scale. The demo stores nothing, so this counter is its only record. Expect a low, steady count from the docs, demos and testing; a spike is ops/drift-test.md 9.3. Demo reports dropped: reports of demo sessions from extenders that predate NoReport (E4), which the api drops unstored; they shrink as extenders update (ops 8). Counted per process, whose series are keyed by instance, and read as each process's count over the window, summed: its last value in the window less its last value before it, or its whole value when it began within the window. A drift counter's series starts at its first count in a process, which an increase cannot see, and a process that started and stopped within the window would be lost by reading only the current series; drift counts are small, so this counts every one.

panels.title: drift rate-limit refusals per hour
panels.description: Requests the drift test's limits refused (P7, W8): allocations over allocate_limit, 600 a minute per network, answered 429; starts over start_limit, 120 runs an hour per /24 (/48), or demo starts over demo_starts_per_hour, 30 per /24 (/48), which share refused_limit. A /24 is shared by everyone on that network, so a burst here is not always one visitor; a few /24s at the demo limit is someone scripting it (ops/drift-test.md 9.3, 4). Counted per process, whose series are keyed by instance, and read as each process's count over the window, summed: its last value in the window less its last value before it, or its whole value when it began within the window. A drift counter's series starts at its first count in a process, which an increase cannot see, and a process that started and stopped within the window would be lost by reading only the current series; drift counts are small, so this counts every one.

panels.title: drift requests per hour by outcome
panels.description: Every answer to POST /lag/drift-test (allocate) and POST /lag/drift-test/start, by outcome (P1, P5): created, started, and demo for the demo token; refused_<code>, where embed is a network without Embed, disabled a network whose drift tests are switched off, client_token a client's token in place of the network's credential, expired, closed and busy are the token's state, origin a parent origin not allowed, limit a rate limit, and unavailable no extenders or no border file; rejected, a 4xx; error. Mostly refused_unavailable after a deploy is a process without the border file (ops/drift-test.md 5). Counted per process, whose series are keyed by instance, and read as each process's count over the window, summed: its last value in the window less its last value before it, or its whole value when it began within the window. A drift counter's series starts at its first count in a process, which an increase cannot see, and a process that started and stopped within the window would be lost by reading only the current series; drift counts are small, so this counts every one.

panels.title: drift sweep, time since its last pass
panels.description: How long ago the drift sweep last finished a pass, in any taskworker. It runs every sweep_interval, 15 s, so this stays under a minute. The sweep completes the runs nobody reads, and deletes client_ip hashes and old tests (K3, R1), so while it is stopped those runs wait and the privacy deletes do not happen: ops/drift-test.md 9.1 and 10. LagDriftSweepStopped warns past 5 minutes, 20 passes missed, or one pass that ran to its 5-minute task limit, a backlog the sweep cannot clear. The lines mark 1 and 5 minutes. Each taskworker publishes the end of its own last pass, so this reads the newest with max.

panels.title: drift calibration age
panels.description: Age of the drift model's calibration in force (V4): kappa, sigma0 and the relay thresholds, which size every ellipse (V3). The weekly job keeps it under 7 days while each run applies; a failed week leaves the last good one in force, up to 14 days (ops/drift-test.md 6), and LagDriftCalibrationStale warns past 15 days. No value while the defaults apply: before the first calibration, or after every one is withdrawn. The lines mark 7 and 15 days. The stats collector runs in every taskworker and each publishes the same database reading, so this reads the gauge with max across hosts rather than a bare series.
